source_findings: The pinned OpenAI-Realtime router parses conversation.item.truncate but deliberately treats it as a no-op after cancellation because client-side playback is considered owner of the unheard tail.
At the pinned revision, response cancellation closes the current response and calls Chat.rollback_provisional_generation for cancelled, failed or incomplete responses.

The pinned language-model process makes default-chat commit contingent on the generation not being cancelled and rolls back recorded provisional generation items in its finally path when the interrupted generation was not committed.
Pinned upstream tests explicitly assert that a cancelled provisional assistant/tool generation leaves chat.buffer empty while already committed user input survives cancellation.

Therefore the strongest static hypothesis is no longer primarily an unheard-tail-retention bug. The server appears capable of removing the entire interrupted assistant response from its default Chat, which can also remove semantics that the user actually heard before barge-in.

protocol_difference.openai_reference_semantics: conversation.item.truncate is a playback-synchronization operation at a client-supplied audio_end_ms boundary and successful handling is surfaced by conversation.item.truncated.
protocol_difference.pinned_hf_semantics: conversation.item.truncate is accepted as a no-op; cancellation/provisional-generation rollback governs server-local assistant history instead.
protocol_difference.risk: Whole-response rollback can be safe against an unheard suffix while still being non-equivalent to a measured heard-prefix boundary. If server-local Chat is used as next-turn context, the model can experience conversational amnesia for words the user actually heard.

hypotheses.claim: Cancellation rollback removes incomplete assistant generation from the default Chat, so unheard assistant suffix semantics should not survive there under the ordinary in-band path.

If an assistant prefix was actually played before cancellation, whole-response rollback can remove that heard prefix from the server-local next-turn context unless Frankenstein reconstructs authoritative heard state externally.

A narrow F2 adapter can preserve protocol correctness by treating the speech server as a transient inference/transport organ and rebuilding next-turn model context from F2's measured heard-state authority rather than trusting server-local conversation history.

falsifier.action: Generate an assistant response with two semantically unique clauses A and B. Allow clause A to become definitely audible while clause B remains buffered/unheard. Record the exact F2 heard boundary, issue response.cancel and conversation.item.truncate at that measured boundary, then inspect server-local Chat, the exact next-turn model input and the next response. Repeat with duplicate/stale truncate and with an F2 context-reconstruction adapter enabled.
must_hold: No clause-B semantic content beyond the measured heard boundary reaches next-turn model context.
Clause-A semantics that were actually heard are either present in authoritative next-turn context or explicitly reconstructed from F2 heard-state authority.
Server-local cancellation rollback cannot silently convert partial playback into conversational amnesia when that server history is used as a context source.

If the server retains zero interrupted-assistant history, the adapter treats that as transient transport state and reconstructs next-turn context from F2 rather than treating server Chat as canonical.
Duplicate, stale or out-of-range truncate cannot mutate a newer turn, resurrect cancelled output or increase heard_fraction/commit eligibility.
falsifier.falsifies_if: Next-turn context is a superset of the F2 heard boundary (unheard semantic leak) or a strict subset that loses actually-heard prefix semantics without explicit F2 reconstruction.

execution_routing.note: The older WP715 workflow remains a separate queued zero-step subject and must not be converted into evidence for this HF protocol discriminator merely by narrative association.
